note: HYPOTHETICAL design study. Changes parameters only; the simulator equations and the measured polar are unchanged. No bird value anywhere.

bat_flight_muscle_fraction.source: PMC10966098 (Onychonycteris paper, 10.1038/s42003-024-06032-9) citing Bullen and McKenzie 2004: flight muscle on average 9.13 % of body mass in extant bats, minimum 7.8 %

bat_mech_power_W.source: PMC10154928 (10.1098/rspb.2023.0045): Pipistrellus nathusii, 7.6 +- 0.8 g, estimated mechanical power 0.046 to 0.140 W, mean 0.092 W, from aerodynamic measurement

bat_conversion_efficiency.source: PMC10154928: conversion efficiency 7.0 to 10.4 % increasing with speed in P. nathusii

bat_metabolic_power_per_weight_W_per_N.source: PMC10154928: weight-specific metabolic power 7.1 to 18.7 W per N

bat_inertial_power_W_per_kg.source: PMC9490335 (10.1098/rsif.2022.0315): inertial power about 8 W/kg, roughly independent of speed (Cynopterus brachyotis model); 6 to 7 W/kg in Plecotus and Glossophaga per Norberg

bat_wing_loading_N_m2.source: physics/comparison-data.csv (span-efficiency compilation): Plecotus auritus 6.5, Glossophaga soricina 11.05, Leptonycteris yerbabuenae 14.25 N/m2

pterosaur_hatchling.source: PMC8298463 (10.1038/s41598-021-92499-z): hatchling pterosaur wing loading 15.83 to 17.88 N/m2, aspect ratio 6.1 to 6.5 (modelled from fossils); Draco 22.7 to 24.2 N/m2 quoted there

bumblebee_hover_metabolic_W_per_kg.source: PMC12606204 (10.1098/rsbl.2025.0325): hovering metabolic power 559 W/kg body; overall efficiency 7.3 to 14.7 %

oxycaloric_J_per_ml_O2.source: oxycaloric equivalent for mixed substrate; the bumblebee paper uses 21.1 J per ml CO2 for carbohydrate

bird_values.source: class Aves is the frozen holdout; no bird parameter, comparison or figure is used

mass_kg.reason: same body; the question is what fins and muscle a 60 g fish would need

wing_loading_N_m2.reason: inside the bat range 6.5 to 14.25 N/m2 and below the pterosaur hatchling 15.8 to 17.9; chosen, not optimised

aspect_ratio.reason: kept at the fish value (9.0 to 10.7 in Park and Choi), which already lies in the powered-flier range the pterosaur paper quotes (6.1 to 6.5 for hatchlings; "avian 5 to 12" is a bird figure and is NOT used)

LD_max.reason: same measured polar (conservative: bats are not assumed better)

flight_muscle_fraction.from: not reported for flying fish (Davenport 1992: red axial muscle no more than mackerel)
flight_muscle_fraction.reason: see power budget: 0.16 is the smallest fraction that covers a 1 m/s climb at the bat-derived MAX specific power (0.15 falls 0.05 W short); it is ABOVE the bat mean (9.1 %) and minimum (7.8 %); the bat maximum is not in the fetched sources; at the bat MEAN specific power even 0.16 only just fails level flight

muscle_specific_mech_power_W_per_kg.reason: P. nathusii mechanical power 0.140 W (max) over its flight muscle 7.6 g x 9.13 % = 0.69 g: 202 W/kg muscle (mean 133); a derived figure from two sourced numbers, and the chain may replace it

range.source: PMC10154928: conversion efficiency 7.0 to 10.4 % increasing with speed in P. nathusii

conversion_efficiency.reason: top of the bat-measured range; bumblebee 7 to 15 %

power_budget.verdict_mechanical: design fraction 0.16 covers level flight and a 1 m/s climb at the bat-derived MAX specific power
power_budget.verdict_bat_like: a 60 g fish with the bat MEAN muscle fraction (9.1 %) could NOT fly level at the bat-derived max specific power, and could NOT climb at 1 m/s
power_budget.physiology_note: The O2 demand is what the gill, haemoglobin and cardiac modules must supply for SUSTAINED flight; whether any gill can is for the physiology chain and the Lean O2-to-power bound. Burst (anaerobic) flight for seconds is a separate question. The real fish, per Davenport 1992, has no more red axial muscle than a mackerel.

what_this_does_not_establish: that such a fish could develop (development is not simulated)
that fins of 4x area at the same section keep the measured polar
that any gill can deliver the O2 (physiology chain pending)
